questions.text: A private pilot wants to practice intentional spins in a Cessna 172 that is certified in the Normal category. The POH states the aircraft is 'tested for one-turn spin and one-turn recovery only.' Under 14 CFR 23.2150 and the aircraft's type certificate, can the pilot legally perform intentional multi-turn spins?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — 14 CFR 91.307 permits spins in any aircraft as long as all occupants wear approved parachutes, and the Normal category limitation is a recommendation, not a legal prohibition

options.label: B
options.text: No — Normal category aircraft are tested for one-turn inadvertent spin and one-turn recovery only; they are NOT approved for intentional spins, and multi-turn spins may result in an unrecoverable flat spin

options.label: C
options.text: No — but the pilot can request a waiver from the FSDO to exceed the Normal category spin limitation for training purposes, and the waiver is typically granted within 24 hours

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — any certificated aircraft can perform spins if the pilot has received spin training from a CFI, as the training endorsement overrides the aircraft's category limitations

questions.explanation: Normal category aircraft are spin-tested only to demonstrate recovery from a one-turn inadvertent spin during certification. They are NOT approved for intentional spins. The distinction matters aerodynamically: in a multi-turn spin, a Normal category aircraft may transition to a flat spin as the nose rises toward the horizon. In a flat spin, the fuselage and wing wake can blank the rudder and elevator, making recovery physically impossible regardless of pilot input. Utility and Acrobatic category aircraft are spin-tested for up to six turns and are approved for intentional spins within their W&B limits. Option A incorrectly states pilot training overrides aircraft limitations. Option C incorrectly claims parachutes override category limits — parachutes address occupant survival, not aircraft structural/aerodynamic limitations. AC 61-67C describes the certification basis for spin testing by category.

questions.text: A CFI is providing spin training to a student pilot in a Piper Super Cub (Utility category). Neither the CFI nor the student is wearing a parachute. The spin involves 3 full turns at 4,000 feet AGL before recovery. Under 14 CFR 91.307, is a parachute required?

options.label: A
options.text: No — 14 CFR 91.307 exempts spins conducted by a flight instructor giving training in any flight maneuver required by the regulations for a pilot certificate or rating

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — any intentional spin exceeding one turn requires all occupants to wear approved parachutes regardless of the purpose of the flight or the instructor's qualifications

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — the parachute requirement applies because the student is present; if the CFI were solo, no parachute would be needed, but the student is a non-required crewmember

options.label: D
options.text: No — parachutes are only required above 10,000 feet MSL or when the aircraft exceeds 250 knots, per the general parachute operations regulations in Part 105

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.307(d) provides a specific exemption from the parachute requirement for flight tests and spins when conducted by a flight instructor 'giving training in a maneuver required by this chapter for any certificate or rating.' Spin training qualifies under this exemption because spin awareness is required for the CFI certificate (14 CFR 61.183). The CFI is giving training directly related to a regulatory requirement — no parachute is needed for either occupant. Option A incorrectly ignores the training exemption. Option B misidentifies the student as a non-required crewmember in the regulatory sense — the exemption covers both instructor and student during required training. Option D fabricates altitude and speed thresholds from Part 105 (parachute jumping operations), which is unrelated to in-aircraft parachute wearing requirements.

questions.text: A pilot enters an inadvertent spin while practicing stalls at 3,000 feet AGL. During the incipient phase (first 1-2 turns), the pilot freezes and does not apply recovery inputs. The spin transitions to the developed phase. Beyond the additional altitude loss, what specific aerodynamic change makes recovery from a developed spin more difficult than from an incipient spin?

options.label: A
options.text: In the developed phase, aerodynamic and inertial forces are balanced in a steady state — breaking this equilibrium requires full-deflection control inputs (PARE), whereas in the incipient phase, simply neutralizing controls often stops the rotation before autorotation locks in

options.label: B
options.text: The aircraft's structural integrity degrades during the developed phase as repeated high-G loading from each rotation cycle fatigues the wing spar, reducing the allowable pull-out G-force and requiring a more gradual recovery

options.label: C
options.text: The engine stalls during the developed phase due to fuel starvation from centrifugal force pushing fuel away from the fuel pickup — without engine power available, the recovery altitude requirement increases significantly

options.label: D
options.text: The pilot's inner ear fluid becomes centrifuged during the developed rotation, creating vestibular lock that makes it physically impossible for the pilot to determine the direction of spin — a prerequisite for applying correct opposite rudder

questions.explanation: The critical difference between the incipient and developed phases is the balance of forces. During the incipient phase (first 1-2 turns), aerodynamic forces (lift/drag asymmetry) and inertial forces (centrifugal/gyroscopic) are still competing for dominance — the autorotation has not yet stabilized. Simply neutralizing the controls (releasing rudder and elevator pressure) will often stop the rotation because the autorotation is not yet self-sustaining. In the developed phase, these forces have reached equilibrium — rotation rate, pitch attitude, and descent rate are all stabilized from turn to turn. Breaking this equilibrium requires deliberate, full-deflection anti-spin inputs (the PARE procedure). This is why the incipient phase is called the 'golden window' — every second of delay allows the spin to lock in deeper. AC 61-67C describes the four phases and the increasing difficulty of recovery as the spin matures. Each turn in the developed phase costs approximately 500 feet of altitude.

questions.text: During spin recovery using the PARE procedure, a pilot correctly applies full opposite rudder and briskly pushes the elevator forward. The rotation stops. The pilot then holds the opposite rudder while pulling back to level off from the nose-down dive. What dangerous outcome does holding the opposite rudder after rotation stops create?

options.label: A
options.text: The opposite rudder creates a sideslip that increases the stall speed by loading the wing asymmetrically, making a secondary stall during the pull-out more likely

options.label: B
options.text: The held rudder pressure causes the rudder cable to stretch beyond its elastic limit, resulting in a permanent rudder deflection that requires maintenance before the aircraft can be flown again

options.label: C
options.text: The aircraft may snap into a crossover spin in the opposite direction — the held opposite rudder provides the yawing moment, and the aggressive pull-out provides the stall, meeting both prerequisites for a new spin entry

options.label: D
options.text: The opposite rudder will cause the aircraft to enter a spiral dive in the opposite direction, rapidly building airspeed toward Vne and requiring an immediate power reduction to avoid structural failure

questions.explanation: After the spin rotation stops, IMMEDIATELY neutralize the rudder. Holding opposite rudder provides a yawing moment in the new direction. If the pilot simultaneously pulls back aggressively (as in an aggressive dive pull-out), the AOA may exceed the critical threshold — meeting both prerequisites for a spin: stall + yaw. The result is a crossover spin — a new spin in the opposite direction, entered from a position of already-depleted altitude. This is why the post-PARE procedure is critical: neutralize rudder FIRST, THEN smooth, gentle back pressure to level off. AC 61-67C explicitly warns about the crossover spin hazard and the necessity of rudder neutralization after rotation stops. FAA-H-8083-3C Chapter 5 reinforces the sequencing: stop the yaw, break the stall, neutralize controls, then smoothly recover.

questions.text: You are in uncoordinated flight — the ball is displaced to the right (skidding right) — while simultaneously in a stall. The aircraft begins to roll and yaw to the right. You recognize this as a spin entry. In the PARE procedure, the 'R' step is 'Rudder Full Opposite.' Which direction is 'opposite' in this case?

options.label: A
options.text: Alternating left-right rudder — rapid rudder reversals disrupt the autorotation more effectively than a single sustained full-deflection input, similar to an anti-icing rudder technique

options.label: B
options.text: Full RIGHT rudder — 'opposite' means opposite to the direction the ball is displaced; since the ball is right, apply full right rudder to center the ball first, then apply left rudder

options.label: C
options.text: No rudder — in the incipient phase, the 'R' step means rudder to NEUTRAL, not full opposite; full opposite rudder is only applied during the developed phase after the rotation stabilizes

options.label: D
options.text: Full LEFT rudder — the aircraft is spinning to the right (the ball is displaced right, indicating right yaw), so opposite rudder is full left to create anti-spin yawing torque

questions.explanation: The spin is to the RIGHT — the aircraft is rolling and yawing right, and the ball displaced right confirms a right skid/yaw. 'Opposite' in PARE means opposite to the direction of spin rotation. For a right spin: full LEFT rudder. The full-deflection left rudder creates a strong anti-spin yawing torque that opposes the autorotation. Partial or timid rudder will not break a developed spin — full deflection is required. Option B incorrectly interprets 'opposite' as relative to the ball position rather than the spin direction (and confusingly adds a second step). Option C incorrectly states neutral rudder for incipient spins — while neutralizing controls CAN work in the incipient phase, the PARE procedure specifies full opposite for consistency and reliability. Option D is a fabricated technique. AC 61-67C specifies full opposite rudder as the standard.

questions.text: During the PARE spin recovery procedure, the first step is 'P — Power to Idle.' A pilot argues that adding full power would help by increasing airflow over the control surfaces, making the rudder and elevator more effective for recovery. Why is this reasoning incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: The propeller torque at full power would cause the aircraft to roll faster, but only if spinning to the left; in a right spin, full power would actually assist recovery by opposing the rotation

options.label: B
options.text: Full power increases the propeller slipstream over the tail, but the slipstream pushes the tail DOWN, pitching the nose UP — this FLATTENS the spin, potentially blanking the rudder behind the fuselage wake and making recovery impossible

options.label: C
options.text: The engine is already at idle because the throttle automatically retards during a stall break as a safety feature built into the engine management system of most GA aircraft

options.label: D
options.text: Full power in a spin would exceed the engine's RPM redline because the propeller is windmilling at a speed higher than normal cruise, and the added fuel flow would cause an engine over-speed failure

questions.explanation: In a spin, the propeller slipstream flows rearward over the fuselage and horizontal stabilizer. This increased airflow pushes the tail DOWN, which pitches the nose UP — flattening the spin attitude from a steep nose-down spiral into a more level rotation. A flatter spin is far more dangerous because: (1) the fuselage and wing wake can blank the vertical stabilizer and rudder, removing the primary anti-spin control surface; (2) the reduced nose-down attitude decreases the AOA reduction potential of forward elevator. Additionally, propeller gyroscopic precession can accelerate the spin rate. Power to idle removes ALL of these pro-spin propeller effects simultaneously. This is why 'P' is the FIRST step — it must happen before rudder input to ensure the rudder is effective. AC 61-67C describes the propeller effects in a spin and FAA-H-8083-3C Chapter 5 explains the aerodynamic rationale for idle power in spin recovery.

questions.text: You are practicing stalls solo in a Cessna 172 (Normal category) at 3,500 feet AGL over flat terrain. During a power-off stall, the left wing drops sharply and the aircraft begins to yaw left. You recognize the beginning of a spin. You have never been in a spin before — your private pilot training included spin awareness but not actual spin practice. All four actions below are possible. Which is the SAFEST aeronautical decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Let the spin develop for one full turn so you can confirm it is actually a spin and not just a wing-drop stall, then apply recovery inputs — you need to be sure before committing to PARE

options.label: B
options.text: Release all controls and let the aircraft recover on its own — the Cessna 172 is designed to be spin-resistant, and the POH states that Normal category aircraft will self-recover from inadvertent spins

options.label: C
options.text: Immediately apply PARE: power to idle, ailerons neutral, full right rudder (opposite the left yaw), and briskly push the elevator forward — act in the incipient phase before autorotation locks in, maximizing recovery altitude

options.label: D
options.text: Apply full right aileron to pick up the left wing immediately — this is the natural instinct and works for wing drops in normal flight, so it should work during a stall break as well

questions.sjt_rationale: Option A delays recovery to 'confirm' the spin (get-there-itis) — each turn costs approximately 500 feet. At 3,500 AGL, every second of delay reduces the margin for recovery and pull-out. The incipient phase IS the optimal recovery window — waiting for a developed spin gains nothing and costs altitude. Option B applies ailerons against the spin (macho) — this deepens the stall on the dropping wing and accelerates autorotation, potentially converting an incipient spin into a developed one. Option C assumes the aircraft will self-recover (resignation) — while Cessna 172s are spin-resistant, 'resistance' is not 'immunity,' and depending on CG position and control inputs, the aircraft may not self-recover. Option D is the active professional middle path: recognize the spin entry, immediately apply PARE before autorotation locks in (incipient phase recovery), and preserve maximum altitude for the dive pull-out.
questions.explanation: The incipient phase (first 1-2 turns) is the golden window for spin recovery. During this phase, the autorotation has not yet reached steady state — aerodynamic and inertial forces are still competing. Immediate PARE application in this window often results in recovery within one-half to one turn, minimizing altitude loss. AC 61-67C describes the four spin phases and emphasizes that the earlier recovery inputs are applied, the faster and safer the recovery. The Normal category certification requires demonstration of recovery from a one-turn inadvertent spin — the aircraft is designed to recover IF the pilot applies correct inputs promptly. Delay, incorrect inputs (ailerons), or passive waiting can allow the spin to develop past the point of the aircraft's demonstrated recovery capability.

questions.text: You are turning from base to final at a non-towered airport at 800 feet AGL. You have a tailwind on base leg, and you notice you are going to overshoot the runway centerline. You feel pressure to make this approach work because three other aircraft are in the pattern behind you. All four actions below are possible. Which is the SAFEST aeronautical decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Steepen the bank to 60 degrees to tighten the turn — you have practiced steep turns up to 60 degrees and are comfortable at that bank angle, so it will work at pattern altitude

options.label: B
options.text: Apply inside rudder to tighten the turn radius and align with the runway faster — the other aircraft are too close for you to go around and re-enter the pattern safely

options.label: C
options.text: Abandon the approach entirely and leave the pattern — the traffic density is too high for a go-around, and the safest option is to depart the area and find a less busy airport

options.label: D
options.text: Announce 'going around' on CTAF, add full power, climb straight ahead to pattern altitude, and re-enter the pattern — the other aircraft will adjust their spacing, and a go-around is far safer than forcing a dangerous turn at 800 feet

questions.sjt_rationale: Option A applies inside rudder to tighten the turn (get-there-itis) — this is the EXACT entry sequence for the base-to-final cross-control stall/spin trap: inside rudder (skid) + corrective aileron + back pressure = asymmetric stall = spin at 800 AGL = fatal. Option B steepens the bank to 60° at pattern altitude (macho) — at 60° bank, the stall speed increases by 41%, and at typical approach speeds near 1.3 Vs, this eliminates nearly all stall margin. A steep bank below 1,000 AGL with reduced stall margin is the second most common pattern accident sequence. Option C abandons the airport entirely (resignation) — a go-around within the pattern is safe and routine; leaving the area for traffic pressure is an overreaction. Option D is the active professional middle path: go around, announce intentions, and re-enter safely. Other traffic adjusts — this is standard operations at non-towered airports.
questions.explanation: The base-to-final turn stall/spin is the deadliest scenario in GA traffic pattern operations. NTSB data shows that LOC-I during the base-to-final turn accounts for a disproportionate share of fatal pattern accidents (NTSB Safety Alert SA-019, 'Prevent Loss of Control in Flight in General Aviation'). The mechanism is always the same: overshooting final → rudder to tighten → cross-control → stall → spin at unrecoverable altitude. AC 61-67C identifies this specific scenario and emphasizes that the go-around is always available and always safer than forcing a misaligned approach. The presence of other traffic in the pattern is NOT a valid reason to compromise safety — traffic will adjust to a go-around call.
